author: Vikram Sambasivan
title: Judge strikes down Department of Defense policy capping F&A rates at 15% - The Duke Chronicle
text:
A judge struck down the Department of Defense policy capping Facility and Administrative (F&A) reimbursement rates to higher education institutions at 15 percent on Wednesday.
Duke and School of Medicine administrators have previously criticized the White House’s attempts to lower F&A reimbursement rates across federal departments and called the move “devastating.” Currently, Duke has a negotiated rate of 63% with the DOD, which means it receives an additional 63% of a grant’s award from the federal government, on top of the original award amount, to cover facilities and administrative costs.
The American Association of Universities (AAU), alongside the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities (APLU), American Council on Education (ACE) and 12 universities filed the lawsuit against the DOD, which entered a preliminary injunction against the DOD on July 18, effectively blocking the reimbursement rate cap. Duke — a member of the AAU and ACE — filed a declaration in support of the plaintiffs “to explain to the courts what F&A is and how it works.”
The judge, Brian E. Murphy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, wrote that the policy “is invalid; was contrary to law; and was arbitrary and capricious.” This permanent ruling comes after Murphy issued a temporary restraining order June 17 and a preliminary injunction July 18.
The ruling gives the Trump administration 60 days to file an appeal and applies to “all institutions in all states nationwide in the case filed by AAU, APLU, ACE and 12 impacted higher education institutions against the U.S. Department of Defense.”
F&A rates are the percent at which the government covers indirect costs associated with research — such as buildings, utilities and equipment maintenance — for institutions receiving federal grant funding. Heather Hamby, executive vice dean of administration, defined the F&A costs as “the dollars that Duke receives to support critical infrastructure required to house and administer our research programs” in a Sept. 30 School of Medicine leadership webinar.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth first announced the cap in a May 14 memorandum and claimed it will allow the “DOD to save up to $900M per year” in an effort to cut costs. Hegseth wrote that those funds, which he called “waste” and "bureaucratic fat,” will be reallocated toward “applied innovation, operational capability and strategic deterrence.” Universities say F&A funding is essential to support research and without it scientific advancement cannot occur.
If the Trump administration submits and wins an appeal, the policy will not only affect new grants, but the DOD will also “renegotiate” reimbursement rates on current issues grants — or explore legal routes of “terminating” these awards. Lawsuits are still pending for proposed 15% reimbursement rate caps for the National Institutes of Health, Department of Energy and National Science Foundation.
